story.t: Welcome to the NOC! From here we look after the network of an entire ISP. Today is your first shift.
First day... and why is the video wall flashing red?
Hi, rookie. I'm Z3R0. I'll spend the night taking your network down. Try to keep up.
Easy. Start with the basics: who is who on the network. Every level has a short lesson first, and you can review it during the game.

levels.title: First day at the NOC
levels.goal: Match each device to what it does. Start by tapping the Switch and then its job, on the right.
levels.z: First day? How cute. I bet you don't even know the difference between a switch and a router.
levels.me: I don't know everything yet. But I learn fast.
lesson: A network is a group of devices talking to each other. Each one has a role.
The switch connects the computers in the same place, the local network (LAN).
The router connects different networks. It is what takes you to the internet.
The firewall is the doorman: it decides what can come in and go out.
The access point (AP) is the Wi-Fi antenna. The server is the machine that offers a service, like a website.

check.q: Which device connects different networks, like the company network and the internet?
v: Which device connects the company network to the internet, joining different networks?
To leave the local network and reach another network, like the internet, which device do packets go through?

o.why: The switch connects devices on the same local network.
The access point brings the network to Wi-Fi, but does not connect different networks.

check.why: The router forwards packets between different networks based on the IP address.

levels.tip: Switch = same network. Router = between networks. Firewall = doorman. Access point = Wi-Fi. Server = offers a service.
levels.learn: Every device has a role: the switch connects the local network, the router connects different networks, the firewall filters, the access point brings the network to Wi-Fi and the server offers the services. That is the mental map of any NOC.

left.why: The switch connects the devices on the same local network and delivers each message only to whoever should get it.

left.s: Sits between your network and the internet
left.why: The router picks the path between different networks. Without it, your network does not reach the internet.
The firewall compares each connection with the rules and blocks what was not allowed.
The access point turns the wired network into Wi-Fi.
A server is the computer that offers a service to others: website, files, email, DNS.

right.t: Connects the computers on the same local network
right.why: Connecting computers on the same network is the switch's job.

right.t: Carries traffic from one network to another
right.why: Carrying traffic from one network to another is the router's job.

right.t: Decides what can come in and go out
right.why: Deciding what gets through is the firewall's job.
Wi-Fi is the access point's job.

right.t: Offers a service, like a website
right.why: Offering a service is the server's job.

levels.title: Network layers
levels.goal: Put each piece of the network in the layer where it works.
levels.intro: Every conversation on the network goes through layers, like a letter: the text, the envelope, the address and the mail carrier. Sort each item into the right layer.
levels.z: Networking is a total mess. Nobody gets it.
levels.me: No mess at all. It's layers, and each one has a job.
lesson: The TCP/IP model splits the network into 4 layers. Each one solves a problem and hands the result to the one above.
Link/physical: the medium (cable, Wi-Fi) and the card address, the MAC. The switch works here.
Internet (network): the IP address and the path between networks. The router works here.
Transport: TCP or UDP and the ports, which say which program receives it.
Application: what you use: website (HTTP), names (DNS), email. The 7-layer OSI model is the detailed version of the same map.

check.q: Which layer does the port (like 443) belong to?
v: A port number, like 443, belongs to which layer?
HTTPS uses port 443. Which layer handles that port information?

o.why: The link layer has the cable, Wi-Fi and the MAC.
The application is the service (HTTP, DNS). The port belongs to the transport layer, along with TCP and UDP.

check.why: Ports, TCP and UDP make up the transport layer: they deliver the conversation to the right program.

levels.tip: Cable, Wi-Fi, MAC and switch = link. IP, router and ping = internet. TCP, UDP and ports = transport. Website, DNS and email = application.
levels.learn: Each layer has a job: link carries the signal to the next card (MAC), internet carries the packet between networks (IP), transport delivers it to the right program (port, TCP/UDP) and application is the service you use. When something breaks, thinking in layers tells you where to start.

a.why: The cable is the physical medium: it carries the electrical signal from one card to another.
Wi-Fi radio is the wireless physical medium, like an invisible cable.
The MAC identifies the network card on the local link. It does not cross routers.
The switch forwards frames by MAC address within the same local network.
The IP identifies the machine across different networks. That is the internet layer.
The router reads the destination IP and picks the path between networks.
Ping uses ICMP, which travels along with IP to test if the destination answers.
The port says which program receives the conversation. Ports belong to the transport layer.
TCP confirms delivery and resends what was lost: a transport protocol.
UDP sends without confirming, faster: also a transport protocol.
HTTP is the language of websites: application layer.
DNS translates names into IPs. It is a service, so it lives in the application layer.
SMTP sends email: another application layer service.

levels.title: Address, port and MAC
levels.goal: Classify each item as an IP address, a port or a MAC address.
levels.intro: Everything is mixed up in the NOC spreadsheet. Separate what is an IP address, what is a port and what is a MAC address.
levels.z: I mixed IPs, ports and MACs in your spreadsheet. Good luck sorting them.
levels.me: Street address, apartment number and ID card. I can tell them apart.
lesson: Think of a building: the IP address is the building's street address, and the port is the apartment number (which program will answer).
IPv4 has 4 numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, like 192.168.1.10.
A port is a single number, from 0 to 65535. Some are famous: 80 (website), 443 (secure website), 22 (SSH).
The MAC is the network card's "ID card", burned in at the factory: 6 hexadecimal pairs, like 3c:22:fb:11:0a:7e.

check.q: Which of these is a MAC address?
v: Among the options, which one has the format of a MAC address?
A MAC address is the physical address of the network card. Which of these is one?

o.why: Four numbers with dots: that is an IPv4 address.
A single number is a port.

check.why: A MAC has 6 hexadecimal pairs, separated by colons or hyphens.

levels.tip: Four numbers with dots = IP. A single number = port. Six pairs with colons or hyphens = MAC.
levels.learn: The IP address says which machine, the port says which program inside it and the MAC identifies the network card on the cable or Wi-Fi. They are three different layers of the same conversation.

a.why: 4 numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots: IPv4 address.
IPv4 address of Google's public DNS.
IPv4 address, common on internal networks.
A single number, up to 65535: it is a port. 443 is the secure website one (HTTPS).
SSH port, secure remote access.
Port for the unencrypted website (HTTP).
Windows remote desktop port (RDP).
6 hexadecimal pairs separated by colons: MAC address.
MAC written with hyphens, the way Windows shows it.
Also a MAC: 6 pairs from 00 to ff.

levels.title: Binary without fear
levels.goal: Convert the numbers between binary and decimal.
levels.intro: Inside, an IP is just a row of 0 and 1. Each chunk of 8 bits (an octet) becomes a number from 0 to 255. Use the table from the lesson and fill it in.
levels.z: 11000000. I bet you don't even know what that means.
lesson: A bit is 0 or 1. 8 bits make an octet. IPv4 has 4 octets: 32 bits.
Each position in the octet is worth a number. From left to right: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
To convert, add the values of the positions that have a 1. Example: 00000101 = 4 + 1 = 5.
All on, 11111111, gives 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255. That is why no IP number goes above 255.

v: Converting the binary 10000001 to decimal, what is the result?
What is the octet 10000001 worth in decimal?

o.why: You only counted how many 1s there are. Each 1 is worth its position: 128 and 1.
You forgot to add the last bit, which is worth 1.

check.why: The first bit is worth 128 and the last is worth 1: 128 + 1 = 129.

levels.tip: Positions: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. Add only where there is a 1. 11000000 = 128+64.
levels.learn: Binary is a sum of positions: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. An octet goes from 0 (00000000) to 255 (11111111), and IPv4 has 4 octets, 32 bits. This math is what makes masks and subnets make sense.
levels.html:
Bits in an octet[b]
Bits in an IPv4 address[ip]
11000000 in decimal[a]
10101000 in decimal[c]
00001010 in decimal[d]
255 in binary[e]

explain.b: An octet has 8 bits. Hence the name: octo = eight.
explain.a: 11000000: the first two bits are worth 128 and 64. 128 + 64 = 192.
explain.c: 10101000: 128 + 32 + 8 = 168. That is why 192.168 shows up so often.

chips.why: 4 is the number of IPv4 octets, not bits.
8 bits can count 256 values, but they go from 0 to 255. The biggest number is 255.
10100000 would be 160. In 10101000 the 8 bit is on too: 168.
11111110 is 254: the last bit, worth 1, is missing.

levels.title: What ping tells you
levels.goal: Answer the questions about ping, gateway and DNS to understand the NOC panel.
levels.z: Your panel is full of numbers. I bet you can't even read a ping.
levels.me: Ping is the first tool of any analyst. Let's read it.
lesson: ping sends an "are you there?" to another device and measures how long the reply takes.
Reply in ms (milliseconds) = it got there. Timeout = nothing came back.
The gateway is your network's exit door, usually the router.
DNS translates names (google.com) into IP addresses. If pinging the IP works but the name does not, the problem is DNS.

check.q: Ping to the gateway answers, but to 8.8.8.8 it doesn't. Where is the problem?
v: The gateway answers ping, but 8.8.8.8 doesn't. Which part is failing?
The local network is fine (the gateway answers), but nothing on the internet answers. Where is the problem?
o: On the way out to the internet

o.why: If it were the card, not even the gateway would answer.
8.8.8.8 is an IP: the test doesn't even use DNS.

check.why: The local network works (the gateway answers); what fails is from the gateway outward.

levels.tip: Timeout = no reply. ms = round-trip time. Gateway = network exit. IP answers but name doesn't = DNS.
levels.learn: Ping measures whether something answers and how fast. With it you split the problems: no reply from the gateway is the local network, no reply from the internet is the exit, and a name that doesn't resolve is DNS.

qs.q: You pinged the server and got "Request timed out". What does that mean?
v: Ping to the server only shows "Request timed out". What does it mean?
Every ping line came back as "timed out". What happened to the packets?
o: No reply came back: the server may be off, off the network or blocking ping

o.why: A quick reply shows up as a time in ms, for example "time=12 ms".

o.t: The internet is faster than usual
o.why: Timeout is a lack of reply, not speed.
The cable type doesn't show up in ping.

qs.why: Timeout means no reply came back in the expected time. It can be a device that is off, a broken path or a firewall blocking ping.

qs.q: A ping result shows "time=15 ms". What is that number?
v: Ping shows "time=15 ms". What do those 15 ms measure?
In the ping result, what does the value "time=15 ms" mean?
o: The time the packet took to go and come back

o.why: Speed (bandwidth) is measured in Mbps, not ms.
Loss shows up as a percentage, like "0% packet loss".
Ping doesn't even use a port: it is ICMP.

qs.why: ms is the latency: the round-trip time. The lower, the faster the reply.

qs.q: What is a computer's default gateway?
v: In the PC's network settings, what is the default gateway?
When the PC needs to talk to another network, which device does it send the packets to? That is the default gateway, which is:
o: The device, usually the router, through which packets leave for other networks

o.t: The server that stores the files
o.why: That is a file server.

o.t: The cable that connects the computer to the wall
o.why: The cable is the physical medium, not an exit address.

o.t: The site that opens when the browser starts
o.why: That is the home page, not the gateway.

qs.why: Everything that is not on your local network goes to the gateway, which forwards it outward.

qs.q: ping 8.8.8.8 answers, but ping google.com gives an error. Where is the most likely problem?
v: Pinging the IP 8.8.8.8 works, but ping google.com fails. What is the most likely cause?
By IP the internet answers; by name, it doesn't. What probably has the problem?
o: In DNS, which translates the name into an IP

o.why: With a bad cable, not even ping to 8.8.8.8 would answer.
The ping never left: the name was never translated.
The monitor has nothing to do with the network.

qs.why: If the IP answers, the connection works. What failed was translating the name: DNS.

levels.title: Who gave me this IP?
levels.cap: Plugging a new laptop into the network...
levels.goal: Build the DHCP conversation, from the request to the confirmation.
levels.intro: You turn on the laptop and, in seconds, it has an IP, gateway and DNS. DHCP did that. Put each step of the conversation in the right place.
levels.z: I turned off DHCP for a whole floor. Let's see anyone work with a 169.254 IP.
levels.me: 169.254 is the PC saying nobody answered. I know where to look.
lesson: DHCP hands out the network settings automatically: IP, mask, gateway and DNS.
The conversation has 4 steps (DORA): Discover (the PC searches by broadcast), Offer (the server offers an IP), Request (the PC accepts) and Ack (the server confirms).
The IP is lent for a while, the lease. Before it expires, the PC asks to renew it.
If no server answers, the PC gives itself a 169.254.x.x IP (link-local). It can't reach the internet with it: a sign that DHCP is down.

check.q: The PC ended up with IP 169.254.10.5. What happened?
v: A PC shows up with IP 169.254.10.5. What does that mean?
What does a 169.254.x.x address on the PC mean?
o: DHCP didn't answer and the PC gave itself a link-local IP

o.t: The ISP gave a new public IP
o.why: 169.254 is reserved for link-local and is never public.
DNS translates names. DHCP is what hands out the IP.

check.why: With no answer from DHCP, the device configures itself in 169.254.0.0/16.

levels.tip: DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack. With no DHCP answer, the PC ends up with 169.254.x.x.
levels.learn: DHCP talks in 4 steps (Discover, Offer, Request, Ack) using UDP 67 on the server and 68 on the client, and hands out IP, mask, gateway and DNS for a while (lease). Saw 169.254.x.x? The PC found no DHCP server.
levels.html:
1. The PC with no IP asks by broadcast: "any DHCP server out there?"[s1]
2. The server offers a free IP[s2]
3. The PC asks for the offered IP[s3]
4. The server confirms and lends the IP[s4]
Besides the IP, DHCP hands out[gw]
IP the PC gives itself when nobody answers[apipa]

explain.s1: Discover: the PC has no IP yet, so it shouts to the whole network (broadcast).
explain.s2: Offer: the server sets aside a free IP and offers it.
explain.s3: Request: the PC says "I want this one". If there are two servers, both learn which one was picked.
explain.s4: Ack: the server confirms and the IP is lent for the lease time.
explain.gw: Along with the IP come the mask, the gateway (network exit) and DNS.
explain.apipa: With no answer, the PC gives itself a 169.254.x.x (link-local). It only talks to neighbors in the same situation.

chips.why: First step: the PC looks for a DHCP server by broadcast.
Second step: the server offers an IP.
Third step: the PC asks for the offered IP.
DHCP hands out the complete settings, not just the IP.
Link-local: the automatic IP for when DHCP doesn't answer.
NAK is the server's refusal, for example when the PC asks for an IP that isn't valid on this network. It is not part of the normal conversation.
127.0.0.1 is loopback, the machine itself. It always exists, with or without DHCP.
The Wi-Fi password is typed on the device. DHCP only comes in after the connection already exists.

levels.title: First terminal
levels.goal: Find out why Google doesn't open on your coworker's machine and fix it.
levels.intro: A coworker complained: "Google won't open". You are in a Linux terminal on their machine. Commands are short phrases you type (or tap below), and the computer answers.
levels.z: I took down your coworker's DNS. They think the internet is down. You'll think so too.
levels.me: I'll test step by step: local network, internet and name.
lesson: The terminal is a text conversation with the computer. Almost every network device is configured this way.
ip a shows the machine's addresses. ip route shows the gateway (the line starting with default).
ping tests if another device answers. On Linux, -c 4 sends only 4 tries.
cat shows the content of a file. /etc/resolv.conf holds the DNS server the machine uses.

check.q: Which command shows the gateway on Linux?
v: On Linux, which command displays the default gateway?
To see where Linux exits to other networks (the gateway), which command do you use?

o.why: ip a shows the interface addresses, not the gateway.
That file shows the DNS server.

check.why: In ip route, the "default via" line is the gateway.

levels.tip: Test in layers: ping the gateway, ping an internet IP and ping a name. If only the name fails, it's DNS.
levels.learn: Layered troubleshooting: local network (gateway), internet (public IP) and names (DNS). ip a shows your IP, ip route shows the gateway and /etc/resolv.conf shows the DNS in use.

cmds.why: Shows the interfaces. eth0 is the network card: IP 192.168.1.50 (inet line) and MAC 3c:22:fb:11:0a:7e (link/ether line). lo is loopback, the machine itself.
The "default via" line is the gateway: 192.168.1.1. Everything not in 192.168.1.0/24 goes out through it.
The gateway answers: the local network works.
An internet IP answers: the way out to the internet works.
The ping never started: the machine couldn't turn the name into an IP. Name resolution failure = DNS.
The configured DNS is 192.168.1.250. Worth testing whether it exists.
The configured DNS server doesn't answer. That's why names don't work.

steps.q: What is this machine's IP address?
v: From the terminal output, what is this machine's IP?
Which IP address is configured on this computer?

o.why: That is the gateway, from the "default via" line of ip route.
That is loopback, the machine talking to itself.
That is the MAC, not the IP.

steps.why: The inet line of eth0 shows 192.168.1.50/24.

steps.q: Why doesn't Google open, if ping to 8.8.8.8 works?
v: Ping to 8.8.8.8 answers, but Google won't open. Why?
The internet works by IP, but sites don't open by name. What is failing?
o: The configured DNS (192.168.1.250) doesn't answer, so the name never becomes an IP

o.why: With the cable unplugged, not even the gateway would answer.
The ping to google.com never left: it failed before, translating the name.
The gateway exists (192.168.1.1) and answers.

steps.why: The IP works and the name doesn't: it's DNS. And the configured DNS, 192.168.1.250, doesn't answer.

steps.q: How do you fix it now?
v: What is the immediate fix to get sites opening again?
What do you do now so names resolve again?
o: Point the machine to a working DNS, like 1.1.1.1

o.why: The router works: the ping to 8.8.8.8 went through it.
The cable is fine: the machine talks to the gateway and the internet.
Nothing points to a firewall block. The problem is the DNS that doesn't answer.

steps.why: With a DNS server that answers, names work again. Afterwards, find out why 192.168.1.250 went down.

levels.title: Names become numbers
levels.cap: Opening the terminal on the finance PC...
levels.goal: Find out why only this PC can't open the ERP and fix it.
levels.intro: Everyone opens the ERP (erp.empresa.com.br) except the finance PC. Its internet works. Investigate how this PC turns the name into an IP.
levels.z: I left a little note in a file on your coworker's PC. Their ERP now goes somewhere else.
levels.me: A name becomes a number in two places: DNS and /etc/hosts. I'll check both.
lesson: DNS translates names into IPs. Before asking DNS, Linux checks the /etc/hosts file, a local list of names and IPs.
dig and nslookup ask the DNS server directly and ignore /etc/hosts.
getent hosts shows what the system really uses (hosts first, then DNS), the same as ping and the browser.
If dig gives one IP and getent gives another, the culprit is in /etc/hosts.

check.q: dig shows one IP and ping uses another. Where do you look first?
v: The IP dig shows is different from the one ping uses. What is the first place to check?
DNS answers one IP, but the PC uses another for the same name. Where do you look first?

o.why: dig already shows the DNS answer. The difference comes from something dig ignores.
A cable doesn't change which IP a name becomes.

check.why: The system checks /etc/hosts before DNS; dig ignores that file.

levels.tip: Compare dig (DNS only) with getent hosts (what the PC uses). If they differ, check /etc/hosts.
levels.learn: Linux resolves names first through /etc/hosts and then through DNS (order set in /etc/nsswitch.conf). A forgotten line in hosts jumps ahead of DNS on that machine only. dig and nslookup test DNS; getent hosts shows what the system really uses.

cmds.why: dig asks the DNS server directly: the ERP is at 10.0.0.10.
getent shows what the system really uses. It found 10.0.0.99, different from DNS.
The ping went to 10.0.0.99, which no longer exists. The right IP, according to DNS, is 10.0.0.10.
Found it: an old line points the ERP to 10.0.0.99. /etc/hosts comes before DNS.
Another way to ask DNS. The 10.0.0.53 server answers 10.0.0.10, the right IP.
The configured DNS is 10.0.0.53, the same as the other PCs. DNS is not the problem.

steps.q: Which IP does the DNS server answer for erp.empresa.com.br?
v: According to the DNS server, what is the IP of erp.empresa.com.br?
Which address does DNS return for the name erp.empresa.com.br?

o.why: That one comes from /etc/hosts. dig asks DNS directly and ignores the file.
That is the DNS server's address, not its answer.

steps.why: dig and nslookup show the DNS answer: 10.0.0.10.

steps.q: Why does this PC's ping go to 10.0.0.99?
v: What makes this PC's ping go to 10.0.0.99?
DNS says 10.0.0.10, but ping goes to 10.0.0.99. Why?
o: An old line in /etc/hosts jumps ahead of DNS

o.t: The DNS server has the wrong IP
o.why: dig and nslookup show 10.0.0.10, the right one. DNS is fine.
With a loose cable, DNS wouldn't even answer dig.

steps.why: The system checks /etc/hosts before DNS. The forgotten test line redirects the name on this PC only.

v: What is the fix so the PC uses the right ERP IP?
What do you do so this PC goes back to using DNS for the ERP?

o.why: DNS already answers correctly. And /etc/hosts would still come before any DNS.
The problem is a file on this PC. Restarting the router takes everyone down for nothing.

steps.why: Without the old line, the PC asks DNS and gets the right IP.
